en: Now begins the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Musical Performance of the Artful Dialogue Arising from the First Encounter."
[1] Now, at the commencement of this aesthetic flavor (rasa), I offer this request while making known my own solemn oath:
if, by writing that "all the development of rasa exists in my own poem," I have here clearly revealed the secret of my intention out of boldness;
Therefore, this [account] of Govinda’s wandering through the lonely forest paths of Vraja should be imparted only into the ears of a worthy person, and not in a public assembly.

Thus it was said. [Śikhariṇī meter] [2] Now, as the night-talk was being composed into a continuous narrative, Madhukaṇṭha, even while leaning upon Snigdhakaṇṭha, spoke, first manifesting this with palms joined in reverence:
The rāsa-sport took place at night;
may its narration clearly become likewise,
for whatever is the cause of something, such is its nature.
Its state is considered to be of that same nature.
[In the Rathoddhatā meter] [3] Having heard this and gazed upon it with joy, they all said: "This which has been spoken is indeed endowed with reason,
for that which is the supreme stream of aesthetic flavor— "

If that [momentary entity] undergoes disintegration in the middle, it cannot attain its own essential nature at all, because of the absence of a connection between what precedes and what follows. [In Gīti meter]
Therefore, let this be introduced exactly as desired and without interruption.
Madhukaṇṭha said:
"The face of the moon-faced woman is the abundant growth-ground for delusion."

When the festival of Rāsa sought its birth, there occurred for those deer-eyed women a pair of eyes that rolled, and a body that shattered the stability of the circle of slender-limbed maidens— such was the splendor of Lord Hari. (Pṛthvī meter)
Her face is more enchanting than the moon; her eyes are more alluring than the lotus;
her luster provides the first stage for the meeting with the splendor of dark clouds;
she is a beautiful sight, adorned by the loveliness of the Beloved of Ramā.

Then, when the festival of *rāsa* sought its birth, [the earth was born]. (5) Now, according to the previous sequence, after the events described in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.21.17, beginning with "The *pulinda* women were full at the hermitage on the full moon night," Hari, out of a sense of being truly fulfilled, felt a longing solely for the sake of attracting Rādhikā, thinking: "Oh, how is this?"
"Could this have been secretly prepared?
[6] Thereupon, a certain forest-dwelling woman, her body smeared with that same saffron, spoke out of compassion to Śrī Rādhā, whose eyes were like young, reddish lotuses:
"That god of the uneven arrows has been utterly defeated by you, as if by your flute."
"Aha! I do not know how she makes her dry and pierced," [in this *upagīti*].
Then, the celestial nymphs of the forest proclaimed this voice from the sky:
"She is born of a noble lineage, yet she is parched and pierced all over by a heated iron rod."
"O enemy of Baka, surely the God of Love has now realized that this flute is dear to you;
for he has rendered that noble-born woman withered of body and pierced her limbs with his five arrows, all for the sake of pleasing you."
[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] [8] Then, wandering through the forest with agitation, the one wearing a garland of wildflowers beheld this saffron mark upon a *tāla* tree:
"The flame of the Bodiless One, having pierced my mind which is occupied by your exceedingly beautiful limbs..."
On the wall, she has gathered a multitude of the fragrances of the beauty of passion;
thus, though I have perceived her ever-dark luster in every direction and intermediate quarter, even so, O Kṛṣṇa, I have not attained you in your entirety.
JGc_1,23.8 // [Śikhariṇī] [9] Having first observed these observations following that [initial perception], this was deliberated upon by the Subduer of Mura: "Alas, alas!
This script, possessing a unique meaning in its words, belongs to Rādhā alone."
This might be possible;
yet even so, she remains there, concealing her transformation by love through the status of her noble birth.
Therefore, for me, the supreme refuge is the praise of the flute, which destroys all veils.
[10] Thus, having experienced a famine of the nectar of Rādhā and practicing forbearance, he again devoted himself solely to the mendicancy of learning the flute,
wherein even the rains passed as if they were thirst-inducing, and even the autumn increased by half due to the abundance of longing.
[11] Regarding that, he says: As for the secret instruction— just as Hari gradually performed the method of drawing [the breath] during her training on the flute,
so too were those successive disturbances of others long since dispelled by her.
Trembling, reeling, moving from one's seat, or departing two or three steps;
in reality, this consists of exiting, traveling along a forest path, and proceeding on a long journey.
Furthermore—

Whatever training in the flute was then undertaken by Him for the sake of attracting Rādhā, each and every one of those [skills] became perfectly complete, even though it was always encircled by His noble intention.
With my neck bowed and my hair standing on end with joy, I perpetually offer high praise to that very flute.
Oh, she who has repeatedly fulfilled the entire series of Kṛṣṇa’s desires!

[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] [12] For thus, having been eager for the training and examination of flutes during the rainy season, that Kṛṣṇa, awaiting the proper time, perceived that the beauty of autumn had arrived.
And perceiving it, he reflected:
[13] Indeed, if this [nature], which is by its very essence pure, were to become adorned with the play of impurities, then we would recognize it as a row of women.
However, because it consists of the *samaya*, I see it as that which brings even those states of being— which themselves subjugate everything— under its own control.

Just as Rādhā [attained me], so if I am capable of instilling a state of submissiveness even in her by cultivating the infusion of another state of being, then I consider myself to have reached a state of unimpeded power for the purpose of instilling that same state in Rādhā as well.
[15] Reflecting thus and beholding the foremost auspicious omen, he said: "Ah!
Tomorrow indeed is determined to be most excellent;
for—Beholding the lotus-eyed one, who delights with the playful movements of a wagtail, that Creator of mine..."
He will quickly bring about the radiant face of Rādhā’s lovely eyes.
[Upagīti] [16] While experiencing this auspicious omen, as long as the full moon remains, the practice of the flute-playing of the Flute-Bearer was spread everywhere. And then—
Beholding those nights repeatedly radiant with the splendor arising from the artistry of the flute in autumn, and seeing even the jasmine flowers reach a state of incomparable full bloom, that Rāma—
The brother, for the sake of pleasure, took delight with the cowherd women.
[Vasantatilakā] [17] And then, very quickly, the full moon— a lunar day of many digits— approached like a guest to bring about his favor.
There, having learned that it was day, he who delights in forest excursions and wears a garland of forest flowers took the cows and performed the return journey to Vraja in the evening.

Having returned to his own moon-chamber and clearly perceiving that the sun had set while the moon was rising with its host of stars amidst thick moonlight, he, through the particular application of his state of being captivated by her, reflected as follows:
Is this the lunar orb rising together with its dark spot and its surrounding halo,
or is this the face of Kāma shining forth, its luster reddened by anger?
And again:
Is it the lunar orb shimmering before me, as if filled with saffron juice?
Or is this the face of Rādhā emerging from the forest of the Yamunā? [Upagīti] [18] In that case, if this is indeed the lunar orb—
Then this is contemplated: "This full moon, having followed his beloved wife, the eastern quarter, constantly anoints her face from afar with a hand variegated by saffron, as it were."

Under the guise of that [moon], the pure-souled one seems today to instruct me, who am of such a nature, in the state of a youth; for his composition is indeed "Sarvatobhadra" (auspicious on all sides). Furthermore, he is even perceived as if teaching this as well: [Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter] [19] Moreover, he is even considered to be teaching this:
I am Vidhu (the moon),
delighting the people who bestow happiness upon those who seek me, as I move toward the quarters of the sky;
O Moon, why do you hide yourself here?
Is it now directed toward the enjoyment of another's supreme delight?

[Drutavilambita] [20] Thus, in every respect, by the favor of destiny, I am now able to go toward that very quarter which has been made auspicious by the moonlight thickening the moon; for— by this very moon, the entire forest...
"Seeing that every direction is filled with delight,
this omen must be favorable to me; therefore, my journey there will bring auspicious results."
[Drutavilambita] [21] Now, if this face, which is the abode of anger for him who is called Kāma, then the very pursuit of that god of uneven arrows bestows the extinction of fear.
If this forest, the abode of her very splendor, exists right there, then as I enter that direction, it will surely penetrate the very core of my happiness. Moreover:
"My mind is intent on going, and my right eye is dancing."
"Therefore, let my conduct and speech be pleasing to you.
(1.23.18) [Anuṣṭubh] [22] Having thus engraved and finalized this, and having brought together the four princes, Dāma and the others— who were satisfied by the pledge of their friendship—
and having attached them through that means, he gathered the others right there under the pretext of sleep, while acting as their gatekeepers.
Having discreetly dismissed the doorkeeper, Hari, following that very green grove by walking on foot because he held the flute in his hand, descended to the bank of the Yamunā.
Having descended, he reflected:
"This is not the face of one whose desire is provoked to anger."
For if this face of Rādhā,
separated from her lover, were to rise up into a state of brightness, it would no longer be so, since blemishes and the like would then appear as distinct features.
[23] Thereupon, having concluded that this was indeed the one marked by the deer (the Moon), he reflected further:
"The Lord of the Night has assumed the form of a lion to destroy the darkness;
ascending the Eastern Mountain, he illuminates every peak on the mountain. (JGc 1.23.20) [Anuṣṭubh]
But the moon shines forth, imitating the face of Rādhikā;
how then is this heart of mine, which bears her very form, so tormented?
[24] Furthermore, having visualized the moon, he spoke to it:
"O Blessed One of nectar-like luster, do not be arrogant, thinking, 'I possess incomparable radiance in all the worlds.'"
But even all ten of your fingers do not equal the splendor of Rādhikā’s toenails.
[In the *Puṣpitāgrā* meter] [25] Having reflected thus, and having selected a suitable place, he stationed four clever youths at a distance along the path; then,
having himself approached a higher quadrangle and mounted it, he prepared to ascend.
Fixing his gaze upon the direction of Vraja,
placing the flute to his mouth,
and about to play it, he thought first of Rādhā.
I shall indeed bring about her departure; for without it, I perceive the fruitlessness of my reward.
Yet, because of the desirability of her arrival, the coming of other women as well brings an expansion of delight to my mind.
But that very thing which is to be accomplished must be understood as being accomplished in this way:
"Yes, yes; by me, a flute-player proficient in the science of arrows, it must be performed in such a manner that only that [specific note] is infused and drawn forth, and no other."
[26] Having thus deliberated and determined for himself, "I shall play the flute in this manner," when he was reflecting upon it,
they, by virtue of beholding the moon amidst its thick moonlight, perceived this as an immediate realization:
"Alas! This very lord of herbs surely intends today to merely test us who are afflicted by mental and physical ailments, and not to treat us.
Then, at that moment, perceiving something extraordinary marked with the sign of a hare, Vṛndā thought this:
Alas, alas!
Due to the tears shed on all sides by those women from the fire of separation from Kṛṣṇa,
the moon has become dim, as if seen in a mirror.

[28] Then, as if having attained mastery over those women with eyes like those of the *camūru* deer by facing them repeatedly, the moon— proud in its own quarter— caused its own manifestation to be eclipsed by the hundred rays of Kṛṣṇa, which were elevated with pride.
[29] While their minds were agitated with the distress of longing to behold him, they remained thus.
The departure of the fair-browed women toward Hari was joined with the autumnal moon; indeed,
it was joined by him in return at that time.
But by the sweet sound of his flute, he was quickly [overcome].
[In the Rathoddhatā meter] [30] For at that very moment, by means of passion— through the coloring of affection and the portion of its hue— the sweetnesses [were manifested].
Keśava perceived the subtle sound of the flute as it was being played.
(25) [Anuṣṭubh] [31] As for the affection felt there, it was with a throat and eyes full of tears, and with hair standing on end.
Accompanied by Mādhava,
Kṛṣṇa, who was overcome by the mental anguish born of separation from Rādhikā, sang with his flute producing notes so sweet they were fit to be heard.
[In the Rathoddhatā meter] [32]: Just as passion is such, he caused this passion to fall away.
That which reached the heart of his beloved like passion itself—
clearly never tasted before on earth, yet now spreading through his limbs like nectar.
[In the Rathoddhatā meter] [33]: The differentiation of the colors consisting of that clamor is as follows:
"O Rādhikā, whose face is like the nectar of the moon!"
O Madhumādhavī, you who bear the burden of sweetness,
my heart— long cherished by you— now breaks forever, O beloved, because of your virtues.

[Drutavilambita] [34] Then, like Bāṇa himself, being skilled in the sound of the flute, having personally understood her perfected state through this [sound], that foremost of the wise summoned others as well to investigate its logic.
[35] Therein, the analysis of the phonemes is as follows:
"Aha! O daughter of the cowherd, my words are bound by white [truth];
alas, you are difficult for even my desires to restrain!"—thus do I become, overcome with shame before the world.
O dear ones, make that arising a source of great joy!

[Drutavilambita] [36] Now, when the one clad in yellow robes had thus sung this *udgītha*, he perceived that it had reached the vicinity of their ears; and having ascertained their respective inclinations, such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, he turned back those who were intent on transgression and lacking in stability.
They set out,
and there they remained facing toward Kṛṣṇa alone,
not toward anything else at all. For instance:
Having forgotten their respective duties in whatever task they were engaged, those women— whose divine eyes were fixed upon the sound of his flute—
rushed toward him, whose splendor was visible, with tears of water [falling from their eyes].
[He beheld] his own lord of life as being composed of the river Srotasvatī.
And at that time—
for those lotus-eyed maidens of Gokula—
Then the Lord of the Night-lotuses caused the night-lotus ponds to experience a hundredfold supreme joy. (JGc 1.23.31) [Āryā metre]
And at that time—some wives, though restrained from departing, remained intent on serving their husbands;
they filled Kṛṣṇa with their presence right there—thus it was spoken by the sage. (JGc 1.23.32) [Anuṣṭubh]
[37] And here, with a tender voice, he thought within himself:
"Indeed, these very practices of the practitioners, performed by the excellent sages who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest as seen in the *Padmottara-khaṇḍa*,
are now equal to the desired and most cherished goals of the most illustrious ones, such as Rādhikā and her other eternal consorts."
Since it is established that they have attained Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the same way as those who had not yet attained Him would do upon attaining Him, [it is said]:

"Even though they were united with that very Supreme Self through the perception of Him as a lover, their bonds were instantly destroyed and they cast off their bodies composed of the material modes. [BhP 10.29.11]
Thus, this alone is sufficient for practice.
And it is said in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa* (272.167):
"All of them attained womanhood and were born in Gokula."
"Having attained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.

(BhP 10.33.38) However, it should be understood that, according to the direction stated in "They indeed felt no envy toward Kṛṣṇa" (BhP 10.33.37), His own devotees are not capable of even conceiving such a thought.
And this is in accordance with the verse: "Even by desiring to kill Him, or even by giving her breast to Hari, she attained the state of the righteous" (BhP 10.6.35).

By the words "even with the thought of him as a lover," and so forth, the author expresses through the particle *api* the inferiority of the means, while establishing that the fruit is of the nature of being the most excellent of all.
And this is logical, because: [40]
Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, does not become their paramour— that is, He does not attain the state of a lover—
even though at the end of that [relationship] He attains the status of a husband, bestowing His appropriate wisdom upon them as if He were a lover;
just as He bestowed the state of being cherished upon Bakī by granting her the appropriate [son], even though she desired to kill Him.
For that which is obtained here with the utmost stability through reasoning from the perspective of the "Nurse" (dhātrī) is indeed the fruit.

Nevertheless—this was stated by me previously regarding how that King of Cedi attained perfection: JGc_1,23.33 // [Sragdharā] [41] "This was told to you before: how that King of Cedi attained success."

"Even one who is hostile toward Hṛṣīkeśa—how much more so those dear to Adhokṣaja? Following this principle, a great distinction is observed in them due to their portion of divine love (*prema*). Nor is the notion of a "paramour" seen even among eternal consorts during the manifest pastimes; therefore, only praise is to be spoken of her. For it is said:

That [love] which belongs to Rādhikā and others—the eternal beloveds of the enemy of the demon race—does not attain the praise of that state of being a paramour born from the mind of a servant; rather, that love is eternal.
Having shattered that [servitude] which creates obstacles, he, rejoicing swiftly, [attained] that eternal beloved.
They attained that [beauty], yet he would not wait for another body as if it were something other than theirs.
[In the *Sragdharā* meter: Having reflected upon this, he spoke clearly:
"Then what? Then what? [43]

Madhukaṇṭha said: Regarding the distinction among those who have been consecrated, as it was heard— the moment the flute’s soft notes reached their respective names, the women of Vraja with arched brows suddenly appeared with bodies in full bloom.
Aho! Since he then brought even the bodiless one (Anaṅga) to growth, how indeed would he not cause women to grow by the power of his own arts?
[Pṛthvī meter] [45] Furthermore:
She who possesses swift expansion, who destroys the abode of sentient beings,
who wards off the unassailable peaks of all heavy [obstacles],
and who, though following a single Lord, bestows the excellence of many consorts.
Fulfilling the desires of the infinite world of beings, she follows [the path] that is both a torrent and a waste. //a//
She whose hair is like shimmering moss, who wears earrings as her lotus-discs, who possesses a circle of bright foam from the falling of various flowers,
and whose body is the water with eyes like leaping young fish.
She follows behind, facing her companions who carry only the vessel for the path ahead. (b)
She who possesses lotus-hands with slow-moving stalk-like arms; she whose webbed fingers are like the limbs of young turtles;
she who moves steadily along the banks of the hut built by her radiant and purifying power.
She is the woman who desires the falling of the swarm of bees upon the tree of her thighs.
Resonant with the tinkling sounds of girdles, anklets, bracelets, and other ornaments, she generally delights in the calls of flocks of swans;
her limbs dance in a flurry of rapid, repeated whirling and movement.
She whose movement consists of the arising of dullness that is swallowed up by a state of complete fullness.
Fragile as the shifting arrangement of garments and ornaments, clinging to the momentum that brings about the reversal of various objects,
she is that for whose sake the destruction of all attachment to the self occurs.
And wherein the forgetting of all names and forms is to occur. //e//
Here, Mādhava— the beautiful abode of dark splendor, whose limbs surge like the ocean— is the true husband;
he is one whose previous associations have been severed and who has attained union with the Supreme.
This mass of lotus stalks possesses a heat equal to that of a river. (f)
And there,
in that forest made beautiful by the auspicious one and filled with the radiance of the daughter of the Sun, [Tūṇaka].

Adorned with clusters of blossoms, resplendent with bees and cuckoos, graced by fragrant breezes, and beautified by the presence of the moon; it is certain to possess all virtues and has long been accumulated as a treasure-trove. [The Earth] (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)

Having quickly ascended a jeweled square upon dry land, he was rapidly producing the sweet, melodious notes of his variegated flute with rising cadence; possessing the splendor of a rain-cloud and delighting in garments of lightning rays.
They beheld him upon the earth, his body radiant with the luster of jewels, like the god of love incarnate;
having fashioned Kṛṣṇa, Gaurī stood there surrounding him. (A yugmaka)
At that time, the row [of trees], its heart longing to support him,
seemed indeed to behold a shimmering line of golden-colored creepers appearing amidst the *tamāla* trees.
[In the Vasantatilakā meter:
Then,
having been invited by the flute-messenger, who is a companion to the stream of his fragrance, they were gathered together.
The fair-browed women, brought from afar by the hosts with great devotion, reached his presence;
though they were fed the nectar of his own radiance by their beloved, they attained no satiety, nor did he cease from that act of giving. (JGc 1.23.40) [Śārdūlavikrīḍita]
On the contrary, the young women, possessing fresh artistic grace, radiant and adorned with garlands of shimmering stars,
with their curved glances, produced in the black cakora bird a thirst born of longing.
[46] Then Kṛṣṇa thought there with longing: "Aha!
These are the fruits of fresh youth and the perfection of merit;
they are a series of new wares for me to purchase from my own excellent beauty, and crest-jewels of the Fortune of the Three Worlds."

The life-restoring medicines for the throbbing god of love, appearing as new crescents of the moon to my eyes which have become like white water-lilies (*kumuda*), descend together, bestow their radiance, and shine forth.
This being the case:
The arrow of Kṛṣṇa’s outer corner of the eye, having pierced my own outer-corner arrow along with its body—
"Indeed, he has entered within to shatter the desires of those who long for him"—
thus did they each individually perceive him.

In reality, however, his pair of bee-like eyes, having first partaken of two or three fragments from all those vines as if they were lotus-stalks, roamed with unprecedented wonder upon Rādhā, as if she were a lotus-plant.
She established herself in an unimpeded state.
Regarding that, he reflected as follows:
"The splendor that bestows auspiciousness is the splendor of Śobhā; the supreme Lakṣmī is the Lakṣmī of Ramā."

This very Rādhikā, with her beautiful eyes, is the delight even of him whose own eyes are dark with passion. (JGc 1.23.43) [Anuṣṭubh] [50] This being so, although she experienced agitation by virtue of the surging flow of aesthetic rasa arising from the trembling that blossomed upon the touch of his such-like gaze, she nevertheless bore a splendor directed toward him, characterized by an outpouring of longing.
And here is a verse consisting of question and answer: "Speak of the likeness between Rādhikā’s two smiling eyes, which shed tears upon seeing [Kṛṣṇa], and [the two lotuses]."
Is it perhaps the autumnal, full-blown, dark blue lotus that releases a stream of nectar?

[In the Rathoddhatā meter] [52] Such being the case, although those women standing before him cast aside their modesty— being intoxicated by the skillful art of the flute, which is peerless in its charm— they nevertheless remained devoted to the ascetic vow of the Sage, for they were lovely in their humility due to their genuine nobility.

[53] When Śrī Kṛṣṇa was dwelling in the midst of those distinguished women, he shone forth in this manner: having placed within the range of his vision the arrival of those women— who, though possessing only the most rarefied fragrances, had themselves come forth, intoxicated by the honey of his sweet flute-song— he, with a playful smile, as if ascertaining the purity of their disposition through that kind of inquiry, sought to savor from their mouths the nectar of speech, ever-watchful for the love awakened in them.
And in order to arouse eagerness for them,
he agitated their hearts with words that were pregnant with a request to remain in his presence, yet woven with a manifest display of indifference, as follows:
"O noble ladies, our meeting with you has occurred for the sake of our welfare."
Therefore, I ask: how was this arrival here accomplished without hindrance? Since you have come despite such great hardship, my mind is filled with hesitation;
thus I ask again: what may I do that would be pleasing to you?
// [Śikhariṇī] [54] Thus, because they are either indifferent or expectant toward their own kin— respectively, by concealing their regard or by feigning ignorance—
and because they are generally unable to comprehend his intention, those women remain for that very reason with some underlying meaning unexpressed.
Again, he spoke these words with a jest:
"Even when questioned in my presence, you maintain a noble silence instead of giving a reply."
Then, what appears to be free from affliction for those dwelling in their homes within Your cowherd village, O Blessed One?
//JGc_1,23.46// [Svāgatā] [55] And then, as they were looking at one another with smiles, He spoke again:
I am not capable of understanding this evil intention;
therefore, you yourselves must deal with it here.
Cast aside all hesitation and speak!
[56] Seeing again that they were shrinking back excessively, he expanded them once more by means of a special application of yoga. Then he said:
"If the task is not possible, say 'No'; O you of restless minds, go to the cow-pen of the Buddha; do not follow me on this path."
This forest is most terrible, and the night here is exceedingly fearsome;
it is surrounded by hosts of creatures that are themselves extremely dreadful.

[57] Here, the construction is not that "the path has not been traveled," nor that "it has not been gone upon. Furthermore, in order to connect that very point through a pun, he made a specific qualification regarding the staircase: "For such unrestrained behavior as this is not fitting for those like you, since you have mothers, fathers, and other kinsmen, as well as husbands."
[58] Again, he said with a smile: "Even sons are heard of.

[59] Thereupon, the narrator reflected: "With an intellect following the conclusion reached in the dialogue between Vṛndā and Paurṇamāsī, he has cultivated within himself the mastery of amorous arts."

I shall clarify this according to the opinion of the learned: that because the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the Tāntrika school— which was accepted by the statement, "All [flavors] are the substrata for the aesthetic flavors of autumnal poetry and narrative" (BhP 10.33.25)— would become insipid due to its incompatibility with its objective basis (*ālambana*), this [Tāntrika view] is indeed a mere mockery.

[60] Then he explained that very point clearly: [61] Thus, although he, the crest-jewel of those full of passion, having sounded his flute to sport with them, was from their very birth devoted to their own mother as their husband—
such that the notion of "husband" regarding anyone else was merely a matter of conforming to worldly convention and a vow consisting solely of the desire for union with him alone;

He clearly inferred from the fact that they had conquered deformity through union with another's body that the state of being his own beloveds must have arisen in them; for otherwise, such a transformation would be inexplicable.

Furthermore, although those women who had not borne sons nevertheless engaged in the social practice of regarding the sons of their brothers-in-law and others as their own children—this being merely due to the natural disposition of maternal affection toward any child present—the conceit of kinship toward them was nonetheless [present].
Although he had determined from the words of a trustworthy person that the conduct was indeed external, he nevertheless engaged in various acts of scratching as a mere joke.

Having performed those acts, and considering the fear arising from the persistent search for him even by his kinsmen who were becoming blind with grief, he spoke as if with indignation: "Why do you entertain such fears here?"
And here, either the genitive or the ablative case is compounded.

Furthermore, it is understood that "having seen" (*dṛṣṭvā*) refers to those verses—both complete and incomplete—as they appropriately apply, and that "he describes" (*ācaṣṭe*) refers to those women who are unmarried and those who appear to be married.
Among these, the section concerning the unmarried women extends up to the word *sahajāḥ*.
Even the words ending with "daughters-in-law are heard" were perceived as an unbroken whole;
furthermore, through the blending of the literal meaning and the suggested sense (dhvani), it caused the mind to tremble.
Behold this forest, honored by a divine season with unprecedented blossoms,
anointed with the splendors of the moon, and made to dance by the breezes of the Yamunā;
this very assembly, gathered by the gods, arises for our ritual of sporting.

The Arrangements for the Journey to Ambikāvana [1] Then, as the assembly hall was shining with the light of dawn as usual, Madhukaṇṭha, whose voice was sweet and who had found the opportunity to speak, spoke longingly: "Madhukaṇṭha, listen now to the subsequent deeds of Hari."

[2] Then, in the ninth year of Hari’s reign— the Year of Universal Joy— which was even more distinguished than the previous one, and when the essence of the mountain sacrifice had been completed in its entirety with great effort during this current year, and after several months had passed, the night of Śiva, possessing extraordinary characteristics, drew forth an exceedingly vast assembly of people.

However, for the most part, because of the common association with fame, wealth, and the like, people go joyfully year after year to Ambikāraṇya to worship the Lord of Ambikā and bestow various riches; how much more so during that extraordinary assembly (samā) which is peerless,
where the cowherds have their hearts moved by the illustrious Gopāla, who is as restless as the waves of the river of playful pastimes such as the examination of curiosities?

[4] There, the land of Vraja—the vessel purified by the fragrance of affection for her sons and the protector of the earth—acted as a perpetual sacrificial feast (*satra*) for the wives of the various cowherds, providing them with happiness; thus, she performed a sacrificial journey (*satra-yātrā*) together with them.

To say more: for the sake of protecting the cattle and the cowherd settlement, everyone, with the exception of Upananda, Abhinanda, and others who were occupied with their own duties, set out ahead of the festival day.

Accompanied by musical instruments, songs, and the like, along with showers of flowers and shouts of "Victory!", and by the agitated movements of the throngs of travelers renowned for their longing to behold Mukunda, [the Lord appeared] amidst the manifold manifestations of gods and men.
They advanced toward the forest of Ambikā, pressing in from all sides. There,

Having gathered those beloved ones upon this earth— which consists of the previously established divisions of the cowherd settlements— he caused them to be worshipped by someone as an offering,
and thus brought them once again to the *rāsa* dance; and therein,
that sweetness which had been tasted by Rādhā on the lip of Mādhava—
That very [melody] was experienced following the rhythmic practice of the flute's sweet notes.
And right there,
the rows of slender maidens from Vraja, with their garments fluttering in the pursuit, shone forth;
did they perhaps bear the banners of victory for the union of the Bodiless One?

[62] And on that path, with Rādhā— who had first attained her departure, who was supremely delightful, and who was worshipped by all the Kalpas— Kṛṣṇa, together with her, in private, nourished great joy through playful dalliance with his beloved.

[63] For when that beloved woman, whose heart was exhausted by the heat of anxiety, met her beloved in secret after he had emerged from such calamity, she then, disregarding even the bounds of modesty, embraced him, her face manifesting the *sāttvika* emotion of paralysis (*stambha*).
For a long time he practiced a state devoid of reflection,
and he continued to pursue her in that very same manner.

Then, when the two lovers had somehow been consoled by their friends, the beloved, while casting his own created pool so that it would shimmer before their eyes, spoke to his beloved with a playful jest.
Behold, behold! This mine, Kamalākara, like the ocean, having reached the king of mountains, shall bring forth the lotus-born Brahmā;
like the moon, even by staying in one place, he shall cause the forest of night-lotuses to bloom with his own rays;
and like the wielder of the thunderbolt, he shall be playful, possessing a thunderbolt-like power.
He shines like the Lotus-born Brahmā through the creation of the world;
he is like the Conqueror of Tripura in quelling the pride of the ocean;
and like the glorious Viṣṇu, he is devoted to being the refuge for the circle of the supreme *paramahaṃsas*.
Like Śrī Rāma, he moves about bringing happiness to Rohiṇī;
and what more need be said? Like Śrī Rāmānuja, he removes the misfortunes and sins that cause distress to the virtuous.
Indeed, by composing this lake—which is the expansion of my own performed merit—I have quickly attained the fulfillment of my purpose.
"But since you have not performed such meritorious skill, how will you attain conformity with the virtuous?

[67] Then her peers mocked her, saying: "We have not met with this obstacle through the sin of killing a bull, such that we must perform an expiation for the world as if it were a ritual atonement. [68]
[69] Kṛṣṇa said with a smile: "This is certainly not a bull;
rather, it is an Asura who opposes the Bull (Vṛṣa) while wearing the guise of a bull.
Therefore, because you have taken his side, it results in your own being 'bull-slayers' (vṛṣaghnas); thus, an expiation for you alone is worthy of being performed."

[70] And in that regard, O King, since this very kingdom—which is being ruled by you—is governed according to the principles of statecraft (*rājanīti*), such governance must arise from the people; therefore, that [people] alone is considered primary therein.
[71] The friends said: "Very well;
nevertheless, in whatever way possible, since this fault has indeed arisen solely through your involvement, for the sake of removing it, we must surely act in accordance with what you have done."

[72] Indeed, that lake which has become a pond through the auspiciousness of your presence shall once again become a lake for her who is of the same age; it will be as playful with the dark hue of Kṛṣṇa’s body as the celestial river Gaṅgā;
it will shine with many stars as a row of beloveds belonging to the ocean of nectar;
and it will be overflowing with the joy of devotion to the god Upendra, like the daughter of Sūtrāman (Sarasvatī).
Like a lotus plant possessing the diverse sacred sounds from the mouth of Sāvitrī;
like the form of Umā, the mother who emerged from the King of Mountains;
like the form of Māyā, the vessel of grace within the heart of Hari.

In depth she was like the power of Rāma, possessing a majjanī that hung down with intoxication; what more need be said? She was like Rādhā herself, a woman who brings under her control the full moon of the one near to Rādhā.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, filled with longing, gently raised Rādhā’s chin with his hand with great care and spoke these words, beautiful with a smile:
"If that face were the moon, then this smile would be its digit; if it were radiance, then those [other lights] would be lusterless;
if they were stars, then fie on them! And if those two eyes were present, then the cakora birds are done with.
Thus, from all people, he heard words of self-contempt accompanied by a group of companions.
O Rādhā, having heard in her heart your praises composed of such excellence, she withers away again and again.
[74] Then, having moved forward, all the women of the roads— traversing every path, traveling every way, with their entire bodies trembling—

all together, in the night when darkness was dispelled by the moon, caused the *rāsa* dance to flourish along the King of Mountains (the Himalayas), amidst the forests shining like the king of seasons (spring), a dance spread with an enchantment exceeding that of everything else.
[75] There, the speech of the goddesses was as follows:
"This is lightning, this is Indra’s bow, and this is the fresh cloud;
constantly raining down thick nectar, it draws forth the cātaka birds."
[76] In that regard, his youth and beauty are as follows:
His splendor possesses a dense loveliness born from a multitude of charms; the excellence of his form surpasses thickly emerging pearls and is enchanting, creating the beginning of the universe.
If, in this way, the state of being unconquered belongs to him at all times, or even in his youth,
then who could reach the perfection of poetry when even there, where splendors abound, [his art] is ever-new?

And just as it was spoken by the women of the city and approved by the illustrious Bādarāyaṇa: "What austerity did the gopīs perform, that they attained his form— the essence of loveliness, unsurpassed and not achieved by any other?"
"With their eyes they drink the ever-fresh, unattainable splendor of fame, fortune, and sovereignty, which is the singular abode [of these qualities]" (BhP 10.44.14).
Thus, let some clouds occasionally arise somewhere from the churning of splendors.
"If even lightning flashes so brightly, then let them play like that!
Thus, by comparing them to lightning within the cloud of Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Śuka has clearly manifested their unfailing quality of being beautifiers; behold this manifest truth! (JGc 1.31.49)
And so he described her thus:
with the placement of her feet, the shaking of her arms, her smiles, the play of her eyebrows,
her slender waists, the movement of her shifting breasts, and her earrings swaying against her cheeks;
"With perspiring faces and their waist-knots loosened, the young wives of Kṛṣṇa, singing of him, shone like flashes of lightning within a circle of clouds.
And in that regard, for now: [79] Just as—
These qualities increase moment by moment within Hari and Ramā;
what need is there for me to say here that they do so day after day? For this state remains forever thus.
In her youth, what more could there be here or even there,
since that *carcarī* was born on a night that ended with the pacification of all misfortunes?

[80] This too was a festival of *rāsa*, as follows: "When it is said that the *rāsa* took place previously following the autumn season, then from its very beginning, even the gods provided assistance with musical instruments and the like."
When others later composed [other works], then Hari, Rādhā, and the others composed this [work], which is worthy of being the great collective recitation (mahā-saṅgīta) of all the Jinas. //51//
Above is the host of stars; on the earth is a row of fragrant and variegated flowers; and following that, here is the moonlight, possessing the splendor of diverse jewels.
There, the assembly of those with spotless faces [the gods] is like the moon; thus stands the state of both, which possess the beauty of the stage for the celestial dance.

The celestial forest paths, the earthly wealth of Mount Govardhana, the night as white as the moon, the dance-circle resplendent with various jewels, and the men who possess the beautiful form that serves as the very model for the women honored by Lakṣmī—all of this, surpassed by Rādhikā, is complete; by whom and how can it be described?
For:
That very moonlit night shone forth, that very stage was held in its own balance;
for the fair-eyed one, Kṛṣṇa—who is invisible to the foolish—was indeed his own equal.
Wherein excellence of virtue shines as supreme as beauty itself,
and where Rādhikā, who surpasses all, is like beauty personified as excellence of virtue.

[81] This very essence of the great *rāsa* has been somewhat understood through the scriptures: "On the delightful Govardhana mountain, its slopes made fragrant by the scent of spring blossoms, He stands, yearning for the essence of the *rāsa*. (JGc 1.31.56) Thus it is said.

[82] Then, at the very dawn of that night of the spring *rāsa*-pastime, Śrī Rādhā—having performed worship with countless companions and being crowded by their assistance—leaped into that charming pond held in her lotus-like hands in order to encompass all happiness;
therein, the fragrance of the bliss of those two beloveds blossomed forth abundantly. For instance:
Sometimes Hari sports in the waters of the pool, sometimes outside,
sometimes within a bower, and at other times in the circle of the rāsa dance;
together with the goddess Rādhā, he bestows happiness upon the entire assembly of his friends.
In the past, that [object] constantly reminded our own minds of it from all sides.
[83] Why say more? On this matter, there is even this verse from the Purāṇas:
"Just as Rādhā is dear to Viṣṇu, so too is her pool dear to him;
among all the gopīs, she alone is Viṣṇu’s most beloved. Thus it is said.
[84] Again, summoning his mindfulness, he spoke this verse upon entering into meditative absorption:

"Because even their meeting with a mutual longing for union was not an obstacle due to the generosity of that [meeting], and because of the joy arising from that, the playful meeting of the two Kuṇḍas occurred;
and because she stood in the midst of all the gopīs with such brilliance during the intervals of the rāsa dance, my mind—even today—does not at all abandon Śrī Rādhā and Her Conqueror (Kṛṣṇa)."
[85] Thus, falling into a state of helplessness and dependence, as if sinking, fainting, and losing consciousness, he, with a tender voice, meditated upon all those various abodes of existence.
[86] And that was appropriate,
for his own mind was such as it had never been before.
It is exceedingly rare and deeply pleasing;
that very conduct becomes ever more fresh as it is experienced again and again.
[87] Having described this, Snigdhakaṇṭha concluded, saying:
"O Rādhā, your beloved is indeed very difficult for all to obtain;
yet he who is now easily accessible is one whom you consider otherwise."

[88] Then, although their minds were somewhat pacified by conciliation, they underwent many transformations; nevertheless, Rādhā’s lover (Kṛṣṇa) and the others— having made common cause and transcended all natural dispositions through their compassionate nature toward every assembly— quickly gratified the charioteer and the prince with gifts of honor that surpassed the path of all desires and consisted of the very essence of every beautiful, auspicious, and wholesome attire.
And they attained prosperity through auspicious blessings;
thereafter, just as before, they all returned to their own abodes, and experiencing those various things even in their dreams, they reached the beginning of the day as if waking from their deeds.
Thus ends [the section] following the Śrī-Gopāla-Campū.

[1] Praise of the Destruction of Keśin. Now, furthermore, we shall duly expand upon the morning discourse as follows:
[2] Madhukaṇṭha, at first, without making a sound from his throat, reflected thus in his mind with complete clarity:

[3] Immediately following this, although those among us who had indeed been blackened by praise from childhood were close to praising Kaṃsa— those whose feet are like the best of celestial sages raining down the bliss of the Lord’s pastimes— [4] nevertheless,
for those who follow the governance of the Lord’s pastimes and always uproot faults rather than bring them forth, [there is no such thing].

"The unwise, in that regard, turn even what is appropriate into what is inappropriate"— thus it should be understood that for these supreme sages dwelling in Vraja, who possess the unsurpassed excellence of radiant, non-dual bliss consisting of their own firmly established love, this [description] would not lead to excessive joy; therefore, it is to be studied with a face whose expression is indeterminate.
[5] Then, with some hesitation, he spoke clearly:
[6] "While Śrī Hari was the enemy of Ariṣṭa and Kaṃsa was distressed, no one was sent away for a year;
and Keśī, though departing, was made to enter his own home again."
"Do not harbor enmity in vain.
Then, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, a certain celestial being, possessing the greatest all-pervading knowledge,
though actually hostile toward him, acted as if he were favorable by following the secret conduct of Śrī Vasudeva.
Indeed, because even Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were born as the sons of Vasudeva,
and because they could not be slain due to the resistance offered by them, that wicked one— who was hostile to the virtuous— quickly imprisoned Vasudeva and Devakī in prison with iron chains.
[9] Having restrained the demon Ārva, Arvāmin summoned him once more and appointed him to his task.
As soon as he was appointed, he set out for Vraja and arrived there early in the morning.
Since Vraja had been established beyond the mountain Nandīśvara, starting from the spot where Ariṣṭa was slain, he found it from afar.
And there, as he approached the cow-pen, his hooves— worn down by rubbing against the surface of the earth with their exceedingly sharp and harsh edges—

raised a mass of dust that swirled in the sky; due to the force of this error and his great fear, the clouds concealed the celestial chariots so completely that they hid the various hundreds of māṣa-beans-like ornaments of those vehicles, making them appear as if they were shrinking smaller and smaller than before.
Since they were devoid of that blazing, powerful vigor, those who were once free from decay appeared as if they had become subject to it.
Thereupon, having surpassed the trees with his swift gait, he—along with all the *arva* and *dānava* demons—shaking everything with unabated pride, let out a gurgling roar like a lion’s roar.

And when that roar resounded, the entire assembly of the most venerable elders—which was difficult to penetrate due to the mass of thick branches acting as a formidable thicket, and which was rendered inaccessible by the difficulty of opening the massive door-leaves that were firmly barred with a multitude of great bolts—[was shaken].

The horned cows, having broken away in groups, suddenly fled in haste toward the forest itself with a bounding gait and in great agitation. Without even noticing this, the horse that was the enemy of the gods entered the outskirts of the cow-pen and, neighing all around, pursued that very destroyer of misfortune (Ariṣṭa) according to the manner of his galloping speed.

[14] Then, due to the flight of the cows, all the cattle-owners— led by the head of the herd and overcome with grief— suddenly abandoned their own dwellings and turned their faces toward him with the utmost longing. [15] Even as he proceeded right ahead with great speed, surpassing all of them, the son born after Rāma (Lakṣmaṇa), whose deeds were truly wondrous, was himself filled with wonder as he surpassed even Rāma by his hostile advance against the enemy.
[16] Then, having fallen into a state of total agitation, the leaders of the Vraja people, as he was advancing toward him, tried to dissuade him and spoke these words:
"This steed, with a coat of scales like adamant, is the conqueror of Indra."
Having surpassed the path abandoned by the gods with the roar of your own thundering,
you are like a fresh *tāpiñcha* tree that has become a mere shadow of its former self;
therefore, do not go suddenly before him, right in front of him.
[17] Thus, even between mother and son, when such a great calamity was imminent, this dispute arose:
"Son, where are you going? I am holding the horse. "Mother, alas, he is indeed possessed by a most violent and wicked resolve!"
What will he do to us when he is deprived of his own mount?
Go home; as for me, I am unconscious. What can I do?
[18] And then, her audacity aroused by that agitation, she pointed this out even to the head of the settlement:
"Out of childishness, I did not address you, the master of the house, with such bold words; rather, listen now as I reveal what I intended."
O Lord of Vraja, why do you not immediately take the parched grain together with everyone else, or why do the others not also come forward at every step?

[19] However, Śrī Rāmānuja— the son of Diti who had been made her son by her from time immemorial— hearing that very thing being described, laughed; having reassured his mother, he, the bestower of happiness and the refuge of trust for the entire universe, gazed at him with a sidelong glance for a moment and called him to come to his side.

And he, summoned by the enemy Pūtanā and inwardly humiliated by her splendor, yet out of his pride as a hero not shaken by her, first began to display his prowess against her; advancing step by step with a slowness resulting from the sequence of his backward steps, he eventually covered all the ground available up to the Yamunā.

Thinking that his own prowess would shine forth from afar, he offered the earth and determined to keep Kṛṣṇa as a hostage; then, like the roar of a hundred thousand lions out of pride, the noble Deva, challenging the enemy faction, cried out, "Arjuna!
And then everything—

Unable to endure him, as if simultaneously wishing to seize, tear apart, and swallow him, Kṛṣṇa—possessing the powerful build of a lion—suddenly let out a lion’s roar and seized that bold challenger with a firm grip. While the entire settlement of Vraja stood there in agitation, following his movements, he, beholding him, leaped upon him with a speed called *utterita*, swiftly descending upon him in fury. There—
That very sky, having crossed over it without even a splash, seemed to drink it as he opened his mouth;
thus did he stride with his pair of feet.
And Hari placed that [tail] back against him. Then—
having quickly raised up this [hare], whose feet and tail were bristling and whose mass of thick fur was like a cluster of blossoms—
And he hurled it toward the front of the hundred bowmen, who stood like the earth itself,
as a mass of foam is cast by the surge of the ocean.
Having regained consciousness, he then rose up and,
opening his mouth wide, rushed swiftly at Hari;
he too, smiling, thrust his upper arm into the demon's mouth.
He gave [it] to the great lizard like a serpent.
Like a divine serpent, Kṛṣṇa’s arm clearly grew within the hollow of his throat out of the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*);
even those [serpents] there, as if struck by the flames of his great poison, [fled].
Then his rays fell away through his own splendor.
His teeth fell out, his senses were agitated, and his body trembled;
at that very moment, old age arose as Death itself.
She was indeed waiting.
When that arm of his constricted his throat, then all his limbs went to a state of bursting apart,
as if from grief for that very [arm], which was their ultimate end.
They all, in every respect, have that very [mind] as their support.
Thinking that Kṛṣṇa’s staff-like arm entering Keśin’s throat was indeed the devourer of the world's vital breaths,
his own life-breaths fled.
"This single gate called the throat is blocked;
for my own exit, I shall make them many.
Thinking thus, what will that host of vital breaths do on all sides?
Having thus observed the vulnerabilities, he then set out from there.
When his life-breath had departed from the house of his body,
Kṛṣṇa’s arm emerged, appearing like a guest;
and that house was left bereft of its master.
It has been reduced to piece after piece by fate; what more has been lost?
When he drew his arm from the *keśikaṇṭha* tree,
it returned to its natural state, like a divine arrow at the conclusion of its discharge.
It is considered logical that he called what was excreted before him "excrement";
thus, the grace of Kṛṣṇa that effects liberation for such as these is endowed with reason.
They describe the body of Keśin, once split in two,
as being like Jarāsaṃdha according to some, and like a *karkaṭikā* fruit according to others.

[22] Thus, when the horse-Daitya had attained duality through his physical form, yet non-duality through his true nature, Kṛṣṇa spoke to those of noble mind who, with their minds scattered in joy, were striving toward Kṛṣṇa’s intention:
"Open your mouth at once; I shall fill your entire body."
"I placed my arm around his neck to mount him there and to control him;
had you been dead by that very act, O haughty horse, alas, why did you suddenly commit such a rash deed? Thus [he spoke].
Then Vraja, emitting a tumultuous roar like a cloud, repeatedly and joyfully enveloped the immovable Hari; he,
in turn, shed tears born of delight like rain.
And he brought forth that [child] on the surface of the earth with a radiance like a mountain stream.

[23] Then all those who were possessed of longing, seated amidst the darkness, experienced a multitude of emotional transformations as they embraced him again and again—each according to their own degree of affection’s intensity and sweetness.

Even though there were intervals between them, they considered those moments immediately following to be uninterrupted; and even when he was with another, they regarded that very moment as being with him alone. Thus, through their embraces, they attained a flood of internal change.
[23] Then, after a few moments, having turned their minds away from external objects, they bathed together with Kṛṣṇa while wandering along the Kṛṣṇāghaṭṭa;
which even today the most excellent of holy sites (tīrthas) continue to frequent as the Keśi-tīrtha.

And at a spot very near to where the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā) flows in a contrary direction, they took up a position within a bend of the bank fashioned by a cluster of *kuṭha* trees and rested there to alleviate their fatigue.
This second crossing is called *Cenaghaṭṭa* by the ancients and *Cīraghaṭṭa* by moderns;
for *cena* is the Mathurā dialect term for the pleasure of rest.
Then, having rested, there is this delightful pleasure of praising the destruction of Keśin, namely the "shattering of Kaṃsa."

Having correctly understood him, those people of Vraja, blooming with double joy and exulting as they followed the glorious Lord of Vraja— the illustrious Govinda who finds bliss within himself and is praised by the mouths of bards whose faces dance with spreading fame— first led the way to the cow-pasture.
When the lowing of the milkers arose there, that cry of Kṛṣṇa was clearly perceived,
just like the loud bellowing of bulls.
The sound of the ocean is smooth and deep.

[26] Then those leaders of the cowherds, headed by the crown prince Vraja, having conquered Śakra and accompanied by their respective herds of cattle, returned to Vraja; however, the king of Vraja and the others alone entered Vraja.
[27] But Kaṃsa, even upon hearing of the destruction of Keśin, remained with a distracted mind and, like one paralyzed, did not emerge from his palace.
[28] Now, the conclusion.
This very son of yours, O Lord of Vraja, who has fulfilled the heart's desire of the charioteer,
is the one who here made Keśin a neighbor to Yama.
Thus ends the thirty-second supplement to the *Śrī-Śrī-Gopāla-Campū*, titled "The Praise of the Destruction of Keśin. Now begins the thirty-third supplement, "The Fulfillment of All Desires."

alas, even the very nature of the beloved and the lover was born as its opposite.

"From that comes love for Kṛṣṇa; following that, a sudden movement toward Him; from that, attachment to Him; following that, some inexplicable state of reversal; and from that, manifest passion. O friend, alas! What indeed shall I do? Thus [she spoke].

[14] Furthermore, even if no fault exists in reality, nevertheless, even the mention of such things spreads a sense of shrinking within me; thus, my mental state acts as if to place a barrier between myself and Vraja.

[16] according to the principle that "the loss of debts, wounds, and stains occurs in due time," through my correct investigation and, subsequently, through those people's remorse and their acceptance of sound instruction;
[17] then, having reflected upon this, he again contemplated it with agitation:

By producing an inner radiance of fire, I shall attain the state of being known as "The Burner."

[18] Furthermore, having visualized himself, he says with reference to himself: "In the forests you act as the ladies of the inner court; you act as the female companions; you act as the wild deer; you act as the cowherd women."
O Kṛṣṇa, having been seen by these women with eyes like those of the cakora bird, how can you feel a longing for the moon in another life?

[19] Again, reflecting upon my beloveds: "Alas! Those very drops of tears that I have placed upon my heart—those very ones will, indeed, usurp sovereignty over it, where necklaces were once fastened."
There, having meditated upon Śrī Rādhā and exclaiming "Alas! Alas!", he spoke again:
"O, the slender vine of Rādhā’s body was sprinkled with sandalwood paste mixed with moon-melt by me with affection!"
This very [lotus], withered by immersion in my eyes born of separation from me, now scorches me here.
She who was previously perceived as being like the crescent of the new moon has become like a flame of fire; that Rādhā utterly consumes my heart.
"O Rādhā, I have come here for the sake of love; alas, I am weary! O Śyāmā, how can I endure this?
Therefore, let the functions of my intellect be directed toward Him with devotion."
Thus, [the path] is favorable in some places, but not elsewhere.

[21] Thus, for a moment, he remained silent with his eyes welling with tears. Then again, as a multitude of such reflections arose, he thought: "Alas, alas! How is it that I, being so weak-spirited, once more pursue this expansion of grief? For if I do so, my fragile mind will not attain a state of distance from it. Thus he reflected.
[22] Thus, having suddenly and secretly abandoned that very [state] with such heedfulness, he attained the state of being a companion to his companions;

yet, not out of excessive cheerfulness, he said with a faltering voice, "But I shall spread this news immediately upon dawn," and with a tender throat and a honeyed voice, covering his face with his own garment, he wept aloud.
He remained for a long time without reaching its conclusion;

only after a great deal of time did he desist from it, and having attained Śrī Rādhā, Mādhava, and the others as his own common companions, he spoke this: "Make yourselves happy by performing that very happiness of the self."
"Let that sorrow, which has come through conversation, be dispelled by further conversation.
Thus, when those two had sat down nearby, Śrī Rādhā, Mādhava, and the others— having resolved that sorrow, which was like something obtained in a dream, so that it would result in happiness—
returned each to their respective dwellings.

[24] Then, during the morning conversation, Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "Thus, having subdued the other partisans of Kaṃsa who were engaged in unjust acts—after the slaying of Ariṣṭa and Keśin—the illustrious Govinda, his lotus-eyes opened at daybreak, reflected in his mind: 'Almost all those on Kaṃsa's side have been destroyed; and Keśin too shall fall today or tomorrow.'"
Only the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa remains;
as for others, since they have gained an opening and are indifferent to his preeminence, there is no need for me to go there.
For I am indeed one whose mouth has been covered by my father.
But it is not an independent mantra;
rather, another suitable pretext must be sought.
Very well; it should be concluded as it has come to pass.

Just as those two departed, so too did the entire multitude of people follow them to Vraja;
alas, even the animals placed a thorn in their hearts.
[29] And I am able to declare this as the foremost principle: for— A certain person suffers, while another person experiences happiness;
toward the former there is no compassion, but toward the latter there is compassion. (JGc 1.33.16)

[30] Thus, having deliberated thus in the morning, the illustrious celestial sage, filled with joy, suddenly appeared in person at that very moment when the teacher had dispatched Keśin— who had arrived like a god— to his death, while the Blessed Lord, wandering through the forest for the sake of tending the cattle, was moving about in a secluded spot.
And he saw the illustrious Nārada approaching nearby with his full retinue;
having seen him, who was like the embodiment of the goddess of speech bearing the form of the imperishable syllable,
and like the stream of the Gaṅgā descending from the foot of Viṣṇu.
Like Mount Kailāsa, it possessed the forms of Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and Śiva;
like his own mass of glory, it filled the ears with various songs; and like the ocean of milk, it was perfumed within by the names of Nārāyaṇa and others.
He perceived [him] as one who, by virtue of being within his inner self, bore the splendor of Kṛṣṇa like the moon thick with its full digits;
who, like a mass of autumnal clouds, showered a rain of bliss even upon the eyes;
and who, manifesting the laughter of his own devotees through their particular attachment and devotion, seemed to have brought forth joy itself.
And he saw him thus: like a virtuous lotus in the excellence of constant conduct;
like a tortoise possessing the splendor of a body formed by standing upon the ground that grants all eternal happiness;
and like a banner of victory, adorned with a beautiful girdle upon his shanks.
In the excellence of the name "Sahajānūru," he is like Garuḍa;
in the expansive fullness of his palate, he is like the shore of his own herd;
and in his delightful possession of auspicious beauty, he is like Narasiṃha.
In his having a navel as beautiful as a world-lotus, he is like a lake or like Nārāyaṇa;
in his being clad in yellow garments that are the tongue of excellent qualities, he is like the rays of the new sun.
She was like a peepal leaf in her constant trembling of the abdomen;
she was like a touchstone for blue sapphires in the beauty of the golden lines upon her hips that captivate the heart;
and she was like the ocean, a repository of jewels, in her heart which was a mine of the gems of virtuous qualities.

In its capacity to encompass the boundaries [of the world], it is like the jeweled bolt of Arjuna; in its state of having obtained entry through armlets and other ornaments, it is like the auspiciousness of Kauśalyā’s womb;
and in its state of possessing a shining seal, it is like the sprout of a wish-fulfilling creeper.

In the quality of having a voice and form full of longing, he is like the Pāñcajanya conch; in his servitude to the Moon, the king of the twice-born stars, he is like the Moon itself, the king of the twice-born; and in his beauty that surpasses even the attachment to the face of a parrot, he is like himself.
In his eyes, which delight his own devotees through the vow of truth, he was like a fresh divine fish;
in the creation of his hair, which possessed the splendor of moon-marks, he was like a cloud at the onset of the rainy season;
and in his ears adorned with the crocodile-emblem, he was like the god of love, Makaradhvaja.
He is like the moon in his fulfillment through the cool-bodied form that rains nectar everywhere at all times;
he is like Balarāma in being the delighter of Rohiṇī and Yaśodā;
and he is like Nṛsiṃha in his physical strength endowed with the nature of the Man-Lion.

At times, he was like the Fish [incarnation], manifesting an unprecedented form of pride; at other times, like Vāmanadeva, he shattered the state of being excessively heavy with power through his supreme skill;
and at other times, like Jinanandana, he censured the bull [of dharma] marked by the outcaste of the wrong path.

Furthermore, in his leadership in rescuing the lineage of those sinking in the ocean of milk, he was like Śrī Kamaṭha; in his graceful movement, captivating as that of the Earth-bearer (Viṣṇu), he was like the Varāha incarnation;
and in his destruction of the wicked Kṣatriyas born of Kṛtavīrya, he was like Paraśurāma.
"Just as Viṣṇuyaśas’s son [Paraśurāma] was in his future subduing of the Kālayavanas,
so too was Śrī Rāmacandra in his providing abundant happiness through the composition of Lakṣmaṇa’s life-story.
Thus, these two, which have been mutually considered as excellent points of comparison, are linked through both semantic parallelism (*aikarūpya*) and verbal punning (*śabda-śleṣa*).
The venerable celestial sage, having caused this Śrī Harṣa—the treasure-house of fortune—to be praised through the recitation of the Vedas, announced him to Vikāśa:

"He by whom that Dānava, ever full of pride, was subdued and utterly quelled—he, though supreme, has become subordinate; you, who were once with rising fortune, have now become one whose fortune has declined."
Those children who were laughed at by you without delay, whether with laughter or not—
all those, beginning with Pūtanā, have been purified and made completely pure.
O son of Nanda, you who have attained the state of being devoid of qualities through your very qualities,
it is truly marvelous that you support the earth even while standing upon the earth.
The moon-embodied Śuklā, Sarasvatī as white as the Gaṅgā, and Śyenī—your fame, O Slayer of Baka, is bright; being pure, it makes everything appear radiant.
"Kaṃsa has been whitened by your fame; this, O Kṛṣṇa, is a false statement. There is no contact with him at all, but rather a transformation caused by the fear of him."

O Kṛṣṇa, you too do not observe the connection between what precedes and what follows.
Therefore, I have come to you, whose mind is composed in meditation though you are concealed,
in order to remind you of that divine play which will surely manifest.
In this world, there are many devotees of yours who must be protected by you in due order;
therefore, those divine sports (līlās) necessarily arise in a sequence of before and after.
You are he who slew Keśin, the son of Diti, who dwelt within a horse; you are both existence and non-existence, and you are the one who ordains those other beings who are supreme among the virtuous.
He will become a lofty protector who provides shelter for all.
For indeed,
since those Daityas were rendered as fragile as a mere plaything by you,
Kaṃsa will meet his destruction through the ripening of his own suffering.
That cruel one will seek to take you away immediately, but Akrūra will abandon you;
and you, having left behind your mother and others, will set out to slay him.

[35] Then, having gazed upon him who stood there thus with a change of countenance, the Sage, manifesting another state of being, said: "And so, you have been provoked by Kaṃsa, the reviler of the virtuous, like a jackal provoked by a lion;
for Kaṃsa, like a frog in a well, was merely scratching away at his own itch."
It desires to obtain the friction of your rough, serpent-like arms.

you shall strike him down root and branch; you shall accomplish what was left undone, and while grasping him by the hand, you shall exhaust him through tireless valor until he reaches the limit of rest.
O lotus-eyed one, you will clearly see that elephant, having turned green, being dragged away by those who, rejoicing, pull at his trunk and drag him out.

[38] Here, the citizens sing a verse like one from the Purāṇas: "His eyes, which surpass the blue, white, and reddish lotuses as they bloom, possess a playful flicker that destroys the *khañjana* birds, and manifest the intoxication that crushes the pride of a lion’s pride."

Whose dark-complexioned form, possessing excellent gestures that fashion the arts capable of pacifying the hosts of the wicked, immerses the circles of the virtuous in nectar— such a youth approaches in his fresh prime?
[39] Kṛṣṇa said to himself: "It was indeed rightly said that I would give the kingdom to Ugrasena;
for my return to Vraja alone is what is truly delightful.
[40] And he said aloud: "And then? What happened next?"
The sage said:

"The villagers, the citizens, the kings in the assembly, the gods in the sky who are experts in celestial music, the lords of the gods and others, Brahmā, Śiva, and the son of Brahmā (Viṣṇu), and we ourselves— all are offering praise."

We shall see you two brothers here with the color of tusks from having shed blood, your limbs of flesh unaltered but your wrestling cloths torn away, and you too, O Kaṃsa, swallowed up by the powerful one.
[42] Then, for those who have entered the wrestling arena, there will be this clamor and curiosity:
"What is this dark form—is it sweet or indeed fierce? Is it a woman or not a woman, yet neither divine nor like a garment or a weapon as they should be?"
[43] When Kaṃsa, the vessel of evil, has attained liberation— even though he deserved to be slain— the teardrops from the eyes of women will fall upon the earth and melt your heart.
[44] Kṛṣṇa said: "Alas! Which two did you mean when you spoke of 'my own two fathers'?
[45] The sage said with a smile: "In a former life, this son of yours was born somewhere as the son of Vasudeva."
"The illustrious one is called Vāsudeva by those who possess higher knowledge," so they declare.
Kṛṣṇa, with a wondrous smile, said: "And what after that?

[48] And for the sake of complying with your wishes, and to prevent the Yadus—who are distressed by their flight hither and thither—from gathering together, there will be several days for you who are resolved in mind. Nevertheless, because the royal capital of the wicked King [Kamsa] had long been afflicted by the widespread suffering of Kaṃsa and had thus fallen into ruin, even the once-fierce Ugrasena found it difficult to maintain his composure.

Thinking that such a reconciliation could only come about through his own many past vows, and finding not even a moment’s respite as he delayed his departure for his own Vraja, he deliberated and then approached the Lord of Vraja— who was shining amidst the multitude of his kin in Vraja while traveling together with Rāma in a single company.
Having determined that his own return to Vraja was an unavoidable duty, he said, "You shall indeed go back to Vraja.
Kṛṣṇa said: "Alas!
Will they return to Vraja while actually abandoning me?"
The sage said:
Nanda and the others will regain their cowherd settlement through your supreme and great persistence, but not with their own bodies in that form.
It is clear that the body may be the visible [object], and thus contraction is appropriate with respect to it; however, the Self is not like that.
[53] Kṛṣṇa said: "Alas, what shall I say? [54] The Ṛṣi said: "Your Honor has already declared this; it will be carried out:
'Go, my dear ones, to Vraja, and we too to those who are pained by affection.'"
"We shall come to see our kinsmen after providing for the happiness of our friends.
(BhP 10.45.23) This very assurance of yours will serve as a constant source of consolation for them.

[60] Kṛṣṇa said: "Oh, alas! How vast indeed is the pervasiveness there?

"And you shall obtain a multitude of various prosperities, such as sons and so forth.

"Furthermore, my procrastination will lead to persistence that results in your bondage.
The seer said: "Do not fall into distress;
this is simply your own nature."

Whenever there is a destruction of happiness for my internal limbs—the members of my retinue—I endure it as if it were the destruction of my own limbs, and I bring about the destruction of the suffering of those external to me.
Kṛṣṇa said: "So be it;
let the future story be told."
In this matter, let my own wicked conduct and the news of the suffering in Vraja be set aside for now; let the events of the city be pursued first, by which I,
being deeply affected, will clearly find myself rendered speechless.

The sage said: "Now, your Gāyatra vow itself shall be propagated by Vasudeva and the other Yadu clansmen along with Garga; and wherever you go, Rohiṇī, mounted upon her chariot, shall be led there, but no one from Vraja shall go."

"Because he is a fit vessel for the duties of a kṣatriya, in his creation there will arise for him the suffering of creation, which is rooted in the infliction of pain. [67] Then, saying, "Let us ask another question," he asked clearly: "Thereafter, following those observances and practices, what else shall I practice?

[68] The sage said: "Then, having reached Avantī—the assembly hall where the sciences were kindled by Sāndīpani—you two brothers, being undaunted, shall attain a distinguished lineage through your state of celibate studentship and your abundance of honor, for the sake of acquiring a flawless collection of sciences."
Where, by the mere recitation of it once, you two shall study and retain the entirety of all knowledge, bestowing wonder upon everyone;
where the great multitude of people, sighing, will look at one another with astonishment while praising this [knowledge] in verse, as follows:
"The body is as tender as a young sprout, yet its power is the abode of the highest limit of fortune."
The state of being served by him— Śrī Rāmaṇa— shines forth like a kingdom of the mind joined with equal servants;
he, though intensely coveted even by Vāgīśvarī,
fashioned the woodwork as instructed by his female preceptor through the splendor of bliss.

[69] Thus, in just sixty-four days and nights, you have mastered all the arts; and when you present the teacher’s wife with the fee consisting of bringing back her son—who had been eaten by the five men she had begged for—you will be celebrated among the people as follows: [Text continues...]
Whatever object there may be, whether it be easy to obtain or even very difficult to obtain, let that be given to the Guru;
for that body which belongs to the Guru’s son is as good as lost.
He brought that counsel from which they had previously seen [the truth].
And therefore:
"When you brought back the preceptor’s child even by means of restraint,
then men would have quarreled with their mouths and perished in their hearts."

[70] Kṛṣṇa (to himself): I do not know what the state of Mother and the others must be— those who, having heard people describing that [event], were filled with compassion for me as I was left without support— and which now results in a trembling of my heart.
[71] "Let it be; let us expand upon another topic," he said clearly, "O Blessed One, who is this Pañcajana?
