And you shall take that as part of yourself; however,
whenever you blow [your conch],
your two eyes will become as if moist with tears.
The bliss born from drinking the breast-milk of Yaśodā has been attained through the power of remembrance, owing to the abundance of Your compassion.
[73] Kṛṣṇa said with agitation: "Let another story be introduced, setting aside this subject.
[74] The sage said: "Listen to something else, brief and slight.
You, possessing wealth and learning, having arrived in Mathurā and set out for the glorious Vraja, were met there by your father and others."
Having restrained yourself and reflected that disobeying His command would not be auspicious for the future, you will feel remorse for your conduct; then,

perceiving Uddhava— who shines with the singular devotion to Your own interests— to be exceedingly humble and well-disciplined, you will employ him to produce a state of longing among the people of Vraja, down to their very children.
Precisely because of their shrinking away, you will not be able to bring back the people of Vraja who have been taken by me;

for they will consider this a secret, thinking that since Kṛṣṇa’s desire is limited only to Vraja, his entry into the region of Vraja again will result only in a paralysis born of the frustration of his longing.
Furthermore, the entry of the people of Vraja here would likewise imply their absorption (āveśa). Moreover, that person from Vraja himself will lead them away;
for if he were to say, "We shall come to see your kinsmen," it would result in a violation of the natural flow of your own words, since they are secret and you have said, "But you must not come."
[76] Likewise, even that naturalness arises from such counsel and constraint,
and not through independence.
Furthermore, whatever other hesitation exists in your mind has now become manifest as a lack of approval, even without being explicitly expressed.
He too, while repeatedly carrying out assistance in the avoidance of entering Vraja and other such matters,
will deliver this mantra to the people of Vraja— mantra which, like the Vedas, is independent of others:
"At present, because Jarāsandha and others have formed a conspiracy against your kin, they will, through persistent effort, launch a military expedition with their army."

[78] Likewise, through Uddhava, he sent a verbal message by letter to his father and others, as follows: "Just as you are my kinsmen on all sides, so too do I go to that host of Vṛṣṇis; there, in the land of your life-sustaining affection, I likewise intend to provide protection for you."
However, this form here is indeed myself, yet my very self resides by your side; or rather, the form is within him—for you, the manifestation [of the Divine] alone is the proof.
Furthermore:
What could one who is bound by the ropes of affection say, "I shall come"?
For he who is bound must follow the will—whether it be desire or lack of desire—of that by which he is bound.
[79] I consider it certain that the dispersal of the afflictions caused by the enemies of the gods for Śrī Vasudeva and the others is indeed your own desire.

[80] Furthermore, they shall attain supreme happiness merely by seeing Uddhava before them; for— even in the absence of prior acquaintance, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa protects another devotee by his very sight.
The mere sound of its singing brings joy to the virtuous person.
[81] And thereafter, due to their separation from you, they— pursuing nothing but news of you as their only news—
will pass away quickly, as if months were but days. After having them stay for some months, at the conclusion,
out of regard for the formal greetings through them, they will send word with sealed lips and auspicious faces, as follows:
"This Uddhava of ours, having instructed us that 'you are the Lord,' is now departing;
O son, we do not believe that."
O Lord of Śrī, why indeed does it not please Your son?
Moreover:
O son, even if you are indeed the supreme lord, may [my devotion] nevertheless flash forth at your lotus feet.
And because we always have a longing for Kṛṣṇa, our affection for him persists both here and in the hereafter.
[82] Kṛṣṇa said: "But what will Uddhava say to me?

"Without the rain-cloud, what is the glory of the monsoon; without you, what is the state of Vraja?
[84] Kṛṣṇa said with tears: "Describe specifically the cause for my delay in Vraja.
[85] The sage said: "While you are devoted to your devotees, wearing your armor, and slaying your enemies, even that other interruption will find an opportunity to intervene."
[86] Kṛṣṇa said with agitation: "Alas, what is that?

For this very purpose, you will first dispatch the noble and noble-minded Akrūra as a messenger to a distant land;

moreover, your involvement in the current undertaking shall become even more extensive. For even then, the eradication of Kaṃsa’s faction will be accomplished by you, whether it be already done or yet to be done.

Indeed, because of the truthfulness of their resolve, and in accordance with the numerous promises made by the Lord and His devotees—such as "I shall come" (*āyāsye*) as indicated in [BhP 10.41.17], and "He will come after a very long time" (*āgamiṣyati atidīrgheṇa*) in [BhP 10.46.34], and so forth—it has been proclaimed even by the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* itself.
It is not merely the promise that was made the object of conviction therein; rather, [the fulfillment of that promise was also established].
However, his arrival there has also been established as a fact;
for it is directly perceived in the first statement by the citizens of Dvārakā: "O lotus-eyed one, when did you depart for the Kurus or the Madhus out of a desire to see your friends? (BhP 1.11.9).
And that [statement] is certainly not situated at another time;
for in the *Kurukṣetra-yātrā*, his explicit statement establishes it as belonging to that very time. For instance:
"O friends, do you remember us, out of a desire to accomplish the welfare of our own kin?"

"Having departed after a long time, their minds were intent on the destruction of the enemy faction" (BhP 10.82.41). Thus, he establishes here that the limit is specifically the slaying of Antaśatru by Vidūratha and nothing else. This being the case, immediately thereafter, because an opportunity had been obtained, he revealed to them the manifestation of their own state, which is the natural sphere of their innate nature; and this was set forth in the *Pādma* [Purāṇa].

This too was intended by the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* through the intention of both this person and those others who, immediately after immersing and emerging from the lake of Brahman (*brahma-hrada*), had witnessed that [vision], as expressed in the verses:
"Will it reveal to us its own subtle course? (BhP 10.28.12) and "Wandering, he does not know his own destination" (BhP 10.28.14).
By the statement, "the cowherds to their own world" (BhP 10.28.15),
and by the statement, "and there Kṛṣṇa was being praised with Vedic hymns" (BhP 10.28.18); for this very reason, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Surrounded by calves, heifers, and young kids,
Mādhava always sports within the heart of Vṛndāvana.

And here, the application of constant residence belongs to the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha; for instance, although the Lord of Śrī-Vraja goes elsewhere for the sake of Dhruva, Gajendra, and others—just as the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha does—His constant sporting in Vṛndāvana is not obstructed even by His journeys to Mathurā and other places.
Regarding this, we shall now reflect:
By the logic of *kaimutya* (how much more so), even that Pūtanikā attained the state of a mother through the mere semblance of a connection with her mother's dress.
Near Kṛṣṇa, with the sound of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by cows and cowherds, he will attain that Goloka,
which is exceedingly blissful, difficult to reach, and full of happiness.
Furthermore:
"Vraja, along with all its limbs, its full extent, and its splendor, shall go to Kṛṣṇa;
and whoever shall hold [the memory of] Him together with Kṛṣṇa, following after Kṛṣṇa, and together with Rāma," [he too shall go].
Thus the wise person perceives the Śrīmad Bhāgavata as consisting of exactly twelve sections according to their capacity; for no one else possesses such capacity.
[200] Having reflected thus, the illustrious celestial sage spoke clearly: [201] "When you, having attained happiness from the Rājasūya sacrifice, intend to set out for your own abode,
then Dantavakra— who, through his crooked nature, desires even to conquer Śakra and considers you to be merely a wheel of universal wandering— will, on the road,
seek a mace-duel with you alone, as he is deprived of both Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa."
He will agree to come to Madhupurī;

and having arrived there, while reflecting on his next course of action, he will— after receiving from my mouth the news of your departure toward Dvārakā and the establishment of Śālva— set out immediately toward you, being in a state of great distress.

And at that very moment, by means of my speech— which consists of the power of moving with the speed of thought— you shall have your desire fulfilled as you take that very abode as your own for the journey back to Vraja; and having obtained such a divine chariot, you shall instantly become renowned for reaching the gateway of the city of Mathurā, where you will see the wielder of the mace (Kaṃsa) coming forth.
And as he advances against you, they will hurl maces at you;
yet by that chief of the Karūṣas, the King of Cedi himself, your very life-breaths shall be extracted along with his own vital light, like counter-weapons directed toward you.
And regarding this, there is indeed this verse:
Having defeated Mādhava— who resembles the King of Magadha— in a duel with a mace where our consciousnesses are equal to Bhīma’s,
I shall secure the kingdom of Mathurā.
In this way, who is this Dantavakra that will perish?
And then—
when your own wrath is like the fire of Dantavakra’s funeral pyre,
Vidūratha will become as distant as a cruel insect.

[204] Thus, having caused Dantavakra and Vidūratha as well to suffer the blows of mace and discus from afar, that prince who shines as the sovereign of illustrious Vraja— acting as a guarantor of his own word, a physician for the heart-pains of his kin, and a crowner of his own reputation— will surely summon you, born in Mathurā, back to your own Vraja clan.
Considering that all of this— having reached a state of intense intensity since his arrival from Kurukṣetra, occurring within the temporal limit of his recent journey,

and as if to move Time itself toward once again awaiting the onset of auspicious days— had now occurred on the far bank of the Yamunā, the gods crossed over with their own celestial chariots following his will and [honored him] with flowers.
Suddenly being showered with flowers, he will joyfully enter that dwelling;

and once you have departed, they— recognizing your arrival by the scent wafting from every direction and the distinct rattling of your chariot, and ascertaining it through the diffusion of your fragrance— will conclude that all manner of things proceed solely from your path.

Even without your physical presence, those known as Śrīmat, Nanda, and others, who are constantly engaged in running [toward you], will perceive you— mounted upon your divine chariot like a fragment of cloud within the solar orb— as clearly as a flock of peacocks; and they will experience a profound and intense clamor of joy that is perfectly concealed.

[206] And as they tremble with a state of being possessed by paralysis, perspiration, bristling of the hair, loss of voice, weeping, agitation, and dissolution, they will remain in that very condition, not even perceiving their own movement, far removed from the chariot. [207] You, however, having suddenly descended from the chariot, shall run along their path according to your prowess, honored by all the gods who scatter flowers and play musical instruments.

In every respect, being entirely beyond comparison, you will— through supreme attachment and with unsurpassed power— unite with all of them individually and simultaneously; and embracing them, you will not even regard your own limbs, which are joined to their respective limbs, as distinct from them.
[208] And all those people, receiving you who thus dispel their grief and bestow joy, will become like sons to you, regarding no one else as equal to you.
[209] And so it shall be sung:
"When Kṛṣṇa has departed once more from the city of the Yadus..."

Then the cowherds also bore a flood of joy for each of themselves; for when they were embraced by every person, this distinction was not perceived in the slightest: "Is this Kṛṣṇa, or am I Kṛṣṇa?"—at which time it became perfectly clear.
For it is said:

Just as the descent of truth and dharma is for those at the end of their lives who are devoid of merit, and the movement of rain-bearing clouds is for those standing upon the earth whose bodies have been withered by a great drought; so too is the appearance of a Buddha for the world.

Just as the spreading of the new Gaṅgā refreshes the lakes of Ākūpāra whose waters were drained by the Sage, so too, alas, the essence of union with You is the remedy for the pains of separation from You that remain within the cowherd community.

[210] Then, after a long time, when the individuals of Vraja had finally attained an embrace of You as if they were images, Paurṇamāsī— who had previously remained hidden near Madhumangala and Pūrṇa— along with Vṛndā and her circle,
emerged from their concealment; yet she looked upon them with envy, for they had fallen into a swoon, as it were, from the overwhelming intensity of their bliss.
As if gradually directing their activity outward, she will cause that group to sit within that grove;
and thus they will speak:
"Having placed Kṛṣṇa in the center, his parents, his brothers, and the groups of women..."
His friends and others who had long been associated with his family,
clearly shedding tears as they recalled for a long time his pleasant and beautiful conduct, became motionless and mute from their loss of voice.
[212] But you, there, will satisfy everyone—the women, the young men, the sons and grandsons, the hunchbacks and dwarfs, and even the female and male servants—each according to their needs.
[213] Dāruka, however, standing at a distance like a piece of wood, will look on as if in wonder, being subject to the power of his love for her.
[214] And then Paurṇamāsī, seated there, will speak to them as if she were angry: "Alas! What is this? Why do you act as if you were unaware?"
"How is it that you do not let this man, exhausted on the road, rest?

Thus, filled with wonder and distressed by his fatigue, the mother and father each embraced him from their respective sides with affectionate gestures, while he was surrounded on all sides by everyone else.

You will obtain a courtyard enclosed by a fence constructed from a multitude of carts gathered in the middle of your own cow-pen. Then, all of them, having performed their circumambulations consisting of service to you, will practice only the accumulation of provisions, and not the sequence of formal duties. For it is thus:
O Remover of Sins, when you return from Dvārakā after a long time,
then all these people of Vraja— whether among the elders, the middling, or the lowly— will be dependent upon you.
Alas! Even though they run in every direction and perform this or that single task, they will, in the end, surely reach a state of paralyzed action.
Even if the cowherds are not able to serve you properly, nevertheless, those who enjoy the nectar of your splendor will always protect you.
And from that point on,
the mental preoccupation with one's mother and others— wondering what should be eaten, where one should sit, or where one should sleep— will no longer find satisfaction here. (98)
Your friends, being dependent on pleasure, will forget everything else; but they will remember her, who is so dear to you, and the joy of being united with her once again.
And your servants, O Dāśārha, shall again place their hope in their own bodies,
as they provide for them an immersion in the nectar of service.
The senses, abiding in that state through the power of Your manifestation as before,
shall likewise always bestow delight upon You, O Immaterial One.
Infants, animals, birds, and even fluids—
whatever other beings are dear to you, what need is there to speak of them?
[218] By the power of remembering you, as if you were a tortoise, those who belong to you will indeed remain just as they were before.
Likewise, Baladeva, having departed from Vraja and reached Kuśasthalī, will report this to you.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Harivaṃśa*:
In that very manner, having approached Janārdana in the guise of a traveler,
he shone with a chest adorned by a fresh forest garland.
Then Janārdana asked Rāma, who was seated there, about his welfare in Vraja,
among all his kinsmen, and indeed regarding the cattle.
Then Rāma replied to his brother with these well-spoken words:
"O Kṛṣṇa, all is well with those for whom you desire well-being.
Even though this was the case, at that time, the conviction that you were always residing in Vraja would not have been lost to them.
"The chariot remains standing right there in that very state," [he said] with a sense of detachment.
Furthermore, your peers and elders will inform you of this disagreeable news:
excessive joy is not cultivated in the mind even for a dear friend.
Since he no longer experiences the awakening of passion toward those women who have conceived affection for him as they did before,
and since they, seeing him thus, remain as if withered due to being shrouded by the pain of longing,
your mother, father, and others, hearing this and finding themselves in a state of utter distress, will fall into despondency with their faces turned pale.
[222] But you, who know the minds of mere living beings, having understood that yourself, will inform them: "Why, sirs, do you not yet appear to be overflowing with joy?
[223] And they will all speak with faltering voices: "The cause of our joy is found only upon reaching the path of your realization.
[224] Then you will say: "Certainly; however, regarding that which you doubt,"
This very chariot, possessing a hundred parts, is observed here to be preserved for the sake of accomplishing your purpose along with its constituent members;
or rather, however else you may wish it to be understood, I shall explain it accordingly.

This very thing was already announced by me previously: "Go to Vraja, dear father; we shall come to see our kinsmen who are pained by affection, having ensured the happiness of our friends. [BhP 10.45.23]

"Relatives" means that this dwelling will come about right in your midst; "to see" means that seeing you there is our very purpose in life (*puruṣārtha*). Alternatively, "to see" means to become an object of vision.

Furthermore, regarding the statement: "O Infinite One, Your greatness as a quality may be understood by those whose inner selves are stainless" (BhP 10.14.6), where the phrase "to become an object of understanding" is implied, Uddhava likewise awakened this [realization] within You:
"O Acyuta, in no long time You will come to Vraja."
The Blessed One, the Lord of the Sātvatas, will bring joy to his parents.
"Having slain Kaṃsa, the enemy of all the Sātvatas, in the midst of the arena, Kṛṣṇa makes true that which he promised you upon his arrival. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the Lord of the Sātvatas, though endowed with the perfection of the six complete opulences, will forever bestow upon you two, the parents and lords of Vraja, the supreme glory of happiness in the form of His own constant fondness for nurturing you.
Even there, he will remain indeed unshakable;
for that reason, even today he still makes a true oath— the meaning being that he continues to do so even now.
Therefore, by this very method, I shall discharge my debt of affection toward you, and not even in the slightest degree through coming and going. For it is thus:
[arising] from the repulsion caused by Vasudeva and others who possess forms resembling those of fathers and so forth—

"Out of sorrow, knowing that a swift return would serve to destroy Kaṃsa, I went there; for there lay the fulfillment of my friends' desires and the onset of battle for my enemies. Having thus brought their calamity to an end, if I were to go back now, where indeed should I go? (JGc 1.33.103)
[227] Then, with the consent of the illustrious Lord of Vraja, all those nearby shall also request [this].
"If it is so, we desire here as well, just as in Dvārakā, the expansion of many houses;
otherwise, such a refusal would bring upon us misfortune."
[228] Having heard this and observed the ground, you will think in your heart, as if dissatisfied: "Indeed, these people have reduced the very word 'house' to a synonym for 'wife';

[229] Then, however, you will reflect further: "Let it be."
And the full-moon day, through the swift performance of complete knowledge, shall here create all well-being;

You shall speak what must be spoken.
In that case, Rohiṇī’s mother and Rauhiṇeya’s brother should be summoned from their residence in Dvārakā;
they alone will report everything that has occurred up to this point.
Then, furthermore, you shall inform the charioteer Dāruka: "O charioteer! [230]
"First, having reached the abode of the Yadus with your chariot, bring here immediately His illustrious brother and His mother by means of extreme urgency.
Then, after further reflection, you shall say: 'Ah!
Bring Uddhava as well.'"
Then, when that chariot— which resembles wood fit for His worship— arrives with them after traveling for only half a moment following the wind,

the illustrious Nanda and the others, their minds filled with wonder, will suddenly lead Him to their own home as if He had arrived from Your presence; there, they will cause the entire Vraja to resound with musical instruments being struck with great splendor due to their state of supreme bliss.
And as three or four days pass, Rāma and the others, residing in Vraja, will surely recommend what is appropriate for you;
for how could they— who have thoroughly bound Hari with the bonds of their love and virtues—
act otherwise toward one who is restrained by them?
[233] And all the venerable ones, having gathered together, will decide upon the deliberation regarding the maiden;
for those maidens, Dhanya and the others, are worthy of being considered as being superior to Kātyāyanī.
[234] But Rāma and Uddhava, knowing them to be as supremely proficient as Kṛṣṇa himself, will remain silent.

[235] Then, for that purpose, having achieved their union at the commencement of the undertaking, the husband and wife of Vraja, their desires fulfilled, will reach the vicinity of the full moon; having arrived there, they will immediately offer everything to her, preceded by worship.
[236] She too will say: "That also is indeed auspicious."
"But how could the most excellent gopīs, such as Rādhā and others, not be accepted?
[237] They two, however, will say with embarrassment, "Who indeed are these called Rādhikā and the rest?
She will reply, "They are the daughters of the blessed Vṛṣabhānu and others."
Again, those two will say: "O Guru, pure and so forth—we do not understand. However, let that which is to be purified be explained."

She, however, will say with a smile: "Just as Kātyāyanī is the maidenhood of Ārādhikā and others, so too is she the maidenhood of Rādhikā and the other goddesses. They, in turn, will speak with wide-open eyes: "Let it be told clearly, if even one such as us, though consisting of worldly objects, is made the object of your compassion."
She will say: "Sirs, you are indeed as if not experiencing this;
for those women are still truly virgins even now.
They were merely led away elsewhere as shadows fashioned by illusion."
And that is indeed just like a dream,
because those very [actions] result in beds and so forth as a synonym for the transgression of boundaries.
What is this "something" that I am reporting to you both with direct experience?
Until this very day, those women—devoted solely to him—have remained possessed of great fortitude through consolations such as mine;
but now, they will become such that their lives and limbs can no longer endure even being abandoned by him.
Not only I, but [others] as well, know this of them.
But all the people of Vraja [were affected] by that,
which had already occurred to some small degree even before; however, it became especially intense during the state of instability caused by Kṛṣṇa’s departure from the Vṛṣṇi settlement,
for even the sages will describe this.

[238] In this regard, the former [verse] is as follows: "We did not know how we had been led to such a wretched state by our own delusion, wearing tawny garments... and so forth. The latter, however, is: "Having approached Mādhava, we shall restrain him... and so on.
Having said, "What would our elders and kinsmen have done for us?
they cast aside their shame and wept with melodious voices, crying out, "O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! and so forth.
By such passages as "When Kṛṣṇa’s messenger Uddhava arrived, they abandoned all worldly concerns" (BhP 10.47.9),
and "They were devoid of shame" (BhP 10.47.10),
[it is shown that they abandoned] their mothers, fathers, brothers, husbands, sons, and even their sisters.

This is shown by the passage beginning with, "O Lord, for whose sake we abandon our own kin, who are so difficult to give up, O descendant of Daśārha" (BhP 10.65.11), and also by the passage beginning with, "she who, having abandoned her own kin and the path of the noble, which are so difficult to abandon...
[239]. Herein, as for what was said regarding "husbands and sons,"...
Indeed, I shall explain that by following the secondary (gauṇī) mode of operation rather than the primary (mukhyā), in accordance with the sequence of your questions;
if you should think otherwise in this regard, [please let me know].

Therefore, we explain it thus: because he was brought from hell in the form of a noble youth, he has conquered the abode of the King of Dharma (Yama) and is named Aghajit (the Conqueror of Sin). Although his people are devoted to him, he cannot even be touched or seen by unrighteousness in its slightest degree.
However, his sense of shame alone is sufficient to maintain his boundaries; for in reality, he is not merely [bound] by passion.

Thus, even the seers of mantras have determined that those [energies] proceed toward such a state of being a path, both by virtue of their nature being established from beginningless time and because they are the consorts of Him;
this very point Balarāma and Uddhava know perfectly well, so they too should be questioned.
Otherwise, their role as carriers of messages to those [ladies] would not attain the status of being [true] messengers.
Again, the two of them will say: "Child, what is this you are reflecting upon? She will say: "And he previously reflected upon something."
But Uttara remains knowing [the answer] correctly;
however, for the time being, out of shame, he does not apply his attention.
They will say: "Does he know their desire to sacrifice their lives for that purpose?"

She will say: "He remains knowing correctly exactly what was said," because even previously, during the Uddhava episode, he acted in such a way that they shall sing of those words as the speech of one whose word is truth.
Go, gentle Uddhava, to Vraja and bring joy to our two parents;
release the cowherd women from the anguish of separation from me by means of my messages.
Those whose minds are fixed on me, whose life-breath is centered in me, who have renounced their physical concerns for my sake,
and who have reached me alone— their beloved and dearest self— with their minds;
and those who have abandoned worldly duties for my sake— I sustain them.
O dear one, while I— the dearest of all beloveds— am staying far away, those women of Gokula,
remembering me, are utterly bewildered, overwhelmed by the longing of separation.
"My cowherd women, who are my very self, sustain their lives with great difficulty by some means or other through the messages of my return.

In this context, regarding the phrase "by my messages," it is said: "Having fixed your minds on Me, Kṛṣṇa, and being liberated from all other mental functions, you shall constantly remember Me and before long you will come to Me" (BhP 10.47.36).
The meaning is "by way of conclusions.

Therefore, for those whose vow is to live by a single vow and for their wives, no other destination is appropriate.
Kṛṣṇa said: "And then what? The seer said: "Then those two will bring [the fruit] to fruition."

It is true that even though we have manifested a remedy for the occurrence of worldly conditions that was beyond their capacity, and even though there is the suffering of their dissolution, the desire to make them daughters-in-law does not depart even today;
on the contrary, through constant repetition alone, the appearance of them as daughters-in-law shines forth.
This is observed when there is a deviation from the nature of things (dharma).
Since it was certain that in the future they would come to know the secret, he too perceived that the time had arrived. Then the two of them spoke clearly: "How will people perceive this secret?"
She will say: "This pervasion of the nature of illusion is perceived through its infallibility, in that it inevitably leads to the disclosure of secrets in the future.
She also considered that the time for this had arrived.

[246] Since the secret longing of you two, who prevail over all virtuous intentions, has now reached its highest pitch, it will surely be swiftly fulfilled. They will say: "How do they know that we possess this exclusive devotion to no other?"
[247] She will say: "Previously, you did not truly know that he was indeed your master, even by the words of Durvāsas; rather, you knew it only afterwards. [248] They two will ask: "In what way?

Therefore it has been said: "Alas! Is the noble son now in the city of Madhu? (BhP 10.47.21).
Those two will say: "Those who followed their father-in-law and the others will likely experience remorse.

Then she will speak to him as if he were a man: "How can these supremely virtuous women—who are as sweet and affectionate as honey-wine—be parched by the intense heat of the sun of suffering that is so difficult to cross?"
It must be endured;
likewise, it is to be approved by the virtuous that the bearer of Mount Govardhana—the upholder of his own lineage who is skilled in bearing every burden—is weighed down by the heavy weight of shame.

In reality, however, there is no occasion for even their happiness to be shattered, according to the words of Śrī Śuka: "For your sake, they have surrendered their abode, wealth, friends, beloved ones, themselves, their sons, their lives, and their hopes" (BhP 10.14.35).
Furthermore,
one should not act by striking at the vital points of another's speech, but rather in such a way that it results in nothing but the accumulation of all happiness.

Having reflected upon this, she will speak again with a smile: "At present, a continuous and extraordinary curiosity has surely not occurred to you both—that indeed, in the gambling match with your son Ānanda, he defeated all those who considered themselves their masters, from their wives down to their fathers and others; yet, out of shame alone, O virtuous one, he did not bring them to your house."

"Having been brought there by the cowherds, they were presented to Kṛṣṇa.

She will say: "They too, having realized the truth as instructed by me, completed their duties and pointed this out: [254] [255]

are now directed toward a rival, like those of the female deer!
Desirous of giving, they bear the minds of hunters.

Furthermore,
we do not understand how that desire for the obstruction and contradiction of any other woman could possibly consist of the expansion of love.

Since they have maintained a persistent insistence from our very childhood to drive away our natural affection for him, do not crush us with the weight of your love, but rather grant us exactly what we desire.

And for us who devote ourselves to beholding the state of those most beloved, there is indeed nothing external to that.

[348] Thus, having repeatedly summoned various individuals whose minds were somewhat subdued and who had developed an elaborate devotion, the illustrious King of Vraja, shining amidst the multitude of young women,
brought them into his presence as recipients of his favor and caused them to sit down.
And by that, he caused the entire assembly to shine with joy.
And then—
[he was adorned] with a tilaka-mark on his forehead, with the application of cosmetics on his upper body, with ornaments encrusted with his own jewels, and with divine betel—
Having himself used much of his own excellent garments and garlands,
and having bestowed upon others the carts, draft animals, attendants, followers, and all desirable household goods, the illustrious King of Goloka spoke these two words: *JGc 1.33.126*
From this day forward, let both of you be protected and cherished by me;
likewise, his mother shall be cared for by her mother, and my father by me.

Then, accompanied by shouts of victory, the exalted members of the assembly rained down excellent wealth, having entered that outer hall; for as they went further inward, it was seen that the interior was already filled with such abundance.
Having completed his ritual duties, he indeed dismissed the people whom he had received as his own.

[349] Thus, in this manner, Madhukaṇṭha and Snigdhakaṇṭha shine forth, ever having bestowed the joy of conversation, having always attained the presence of Kṛṣṇa, and being filled with longing to behold His playful charms, experiencing at every moment an intense and supreme bliss.
[350] Although these were not previously described here due to the suspicion that they might be difficult to understand at first glance, nevertheless, in this [work],...
In that assembly hall, which was radiant with the splendor of Śrī Goloka, the illustrious Parjanya sat amidst the priests, occupying a seat assigned to him due to his peaceful appearance.

Bringing joy to all his kinsmen and standing as the leader of them all, he sat there like a rain-cloud showering down every happiness. Within the inner assembly, an ever-increasing and most excellent radiance spread forth.
The illustrious Uddhava was born as the very essence of all; how much can be said of that universal happiness?
Furthermore, let this delightful secret be made known:
among the cowherd girls, who possess the splendor of rows of lotuses in the lake named Vṛndāraṇya...
She alone, known by the name Rādhā, eternally manifests the splendor of the divine *saugandhika* flower;
it is she whom the son of the Lord of Vraja wanders about seeking, and for whose sake he assumes all the various modes of conduct of a cowherd boy,
performing his play with her in every part, like a bee with a lotus.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇacaitanya, together with Sanātana and Rūpa; O Gopāla, O Raghunātha, O beloved of Vraja—protect me! //1//
When the Śaka year, joined with five, four, and sixteen [i.e., 1645], was reduced by ten and yielded a remainder of one,
then this *Gopālacampū* was entirely written by a certain person of humble life who had taken refuge in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
May the forest of Vṛndāvana alone provide all the necessary materials here from every side. //2//
I have for the most part indicated all the pastimes of Hari in their proper sequence;
let them be practiced by great souls according to their respective inclinations. //3//
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Fulfillment of All Desires," following the *Śrī-Śrī-Gopāla-Campū*. //33//
The *Kaiśoravilāsa* is complete;
and thus this *Śrī-Śrī-Gopāla-Pūrvacampū* is finished.
